claim: A filter byte's corner sits on a single pole, and both filters this type's type byte selects are one pole each. The low pass falls six decibels an octave through the middle of the band and the high pass the same the other way; neither is a biquad and neither is two poles cascaded, which would be twelve. The low pass carries the zero the bilinear transform leaves at half the rate, and that is what makes a clock readable off it: the skirt bends from 5.7 decibels an octave between 800 Hz and 1.6 kHz to 10.3 between 6.4 and 12.7 kHz, which puts half the rate just above the top of the band and the rate at thirty-two kilohertz. Read at forty-four or forty-eight it is four times worse and leans. The high pass names the order and cannot name the rate: its corners are all under 500 Hz, its zero is at nothing, and the place a warp would show is its own flat passband. One corner table serves both -- at the four settings both were read the two agree to within 0.064 octaves, which is what this reading resolves.
named: a one-pole section, the same one written twice with its numerator changed
adds: The records say what the cutoff byte did to each twelfth-octave band at eleven settings as a low pass and four as a high pass, and each carries the steepest slope it was running at. What is read out of them here is that those slopes are one pole and not two, that the same is true on both filters, that one corner table serves the two, and that where the low pass's skirt stops behaving like an analogue one names the clock. The records name no filter, no corner and no order, and say so.
refutedBy: A setting of either filter whose skirt runs at a slope no whole number of poles gives, or a low pass whose skirt is still at six decibels an octave at the top of the band, which would put half the rate outside it. Or the same sweep on a corner byte of another type coming back at twelve, which would make the section this type's and not the part's.

rows: Stereo Chorus, parameter 1, Pre Filter (Pre filter), Off, LPF, HPF, LPF+HPF

eraPriors.claim: A pole costs one stored coefficient and a pair costs two, so a part with a sixteen-entry corner table spends sixteen numbers on one pole and thirty-two on a pair.
eraPriors.why: The frequency class argues a table of sixteen corners is affordable and a table of a hundred and twenty-eight is not, and what an entry holds is the quantity that argument is about. Measuring the order is therefore a test of the prior that class was carried by, and it came back on the cheap side of it.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: A skirt on any of this part's corner bytes ran at twelve decibels an octave. The prior is about what a stored entry can cost, and a pair measured anywhere would say the part pays it -- after which a sixteen-entry table is no longer the cheap reading it is being argued to be.

alternatives.reading: The high pass runs at a different clock from the low pass, and the thirty-two kilohertz read off the low pass does not reach it.

separatedBy.observable: The best run there is, and it is not enough. Sweeping the high pass to the top of its corner table rather than the bottom -- setting 127, where the table puts the corner near 8000 Hz and the band set still has room above it -- is where the two rates are furthest apart anywhere this filter can be put.

predicts.thirty-two kilohertz: The approach to the passband squeezed by the warp, 1.08 dB away at 25 Hz from where forty-four puts it.
predicts.forty-four point one: The same curve with that squeeze absent.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: 1.16 dB, which is what the run's own repeats spread at 25 Hz.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: A first-order high pass has its zero at nothing and unity at half the rate, so below its corner the warp is invisible and above it the curve is flat whatever the clock is. There is no setting at which it is otherwise: the widest the two rates ever get on this filter is 1.08 dB, against a floor of 1.16 dB where it happens, a margin of 0.93 -- under one, so the run must not be queued. That is why the four settings on the record return the same median at every rate in the catalogue to a thousandth of a decibel: the reading cannot hear the question rather than the rates agreeing. What would answer it is not a band profile of this filter at all.

alternatives.reading: A conjugate pair sitting at a resonance so low that its corner looks like one pole's, rather than one pole.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The skirt, which a resonance does not touch. A pair runs at twelve decibels an octave however low its resonance is put, and the low pass runs at six over three octaves of skirt where the reading's own floor is under a fifth of a decibel. Scored through the same takes the pair's median is eleven times the winner's and its residual leans.

gates.why: Two things separate and they separate differently. The order is contradicted: a second pole puts twelve decibels an octave where the unit has six, which is a slope the reading resolves several times over, and both second-order candidates come back leaning on both records. The rate is separated on the low pass alone, where the same one-pole section clocked at forty-four or forty-eight is four times the winner's median and leans, and on the high pass the three rates are indistinguishable -- which is carried as a standing alternative rather than as agreement. A third thing separates and it was added in a later round: how the pole is written down. The same single pole written as a running average -- one multiply, one state, no zero at half the rate -- levels off where this one goes on cutting, and on the low pass it is 0.53 against 0.08 and 15.83 dB out at its worst. That reading is not a straw man: a delay's damping byte on this same unit turns out to be exactly it, and each record puts the other's section twelve to sixteen decibels out. So the part writes the pole two ways and which way a byte sits on is a thing to measure per byte.

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// roland-sc8850-01  ·  01 42  ·  filter-section
//
// Generated by yarn sync from inferences/models/0142-one-pole-sections-at-32k.json.
// The claim it closes: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/0142-a-filter-byte-sits-on-one-pole.json
//
// Every constant, every section count and every structural choice below is
// the model's. The difference equations are the ordinary realisations of the
// sections the model names — this site's arithmetic, not a measurement.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#include <cmath>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_42 {

// One pole a filter, at the rate two other classes on this unit have named.
constexpr double kSampleRateHz = 32000.0;
constexpr double kPi = 3.14159265358979323846;

/**
 * A single pole, written either of the two ways the archive tells apart.
 *
 * `Bilinear` is the transformed pole, which carries a zero at half the rate.
 * `OneMultiply` is the cheapest a fixed-point part can write one — one multiply,
 * one state, and no zero — and the archive holds the two as separate candidates
 * because their skirts differ where it can read them.
 */
struct OnePole {
  enum class Side { Low, High };
  enum class Form { Bilinear, OneMultiply };

  Side side = Side::Low;
  Form form = Form::Bilinear;
  double a = 0.0, c = 0.0, k = 0.0, x1 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0, state = 0.0;

  void set(double hz, Side which, Form how) {
    side = which;
    form = how;
    if (how == Form::OneMultiply) {
      k = 1.0 - std::exp(-2.0 * kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
      return;
    }
    const double t = std::tan(kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
    c = (1.0 - t) / (1.0 + t);
    a = which == Side::Low ? t / (1.0 + t) : 1.0 / (1.0 + t);
  }

  double process(double x) {
    if (form == Form::OneMultiply) {
      state += k * (x - state);
      return side == Side::Low ? state : x - state;
    }
    const double y = side == Side::Low ? a * (x + x1) + c * y1 : a * (x - x1) + c * y1;
    x1 = x;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

// 11 settings read, interpolated in log between them and flat outside them
inline double pole0CornerHz(int byte) {
  static const int kAt[] = {0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112, 127};
  static const double kRead[] = {247.223274508, 332.197194043, 419.55398244, 505.808506621, 590.51034386, 961.28389221, 1684.63980924, 2588.22923562, 4025.2845892, 6408.14985161, 8193.18940954};
  constexpr int kCount = sizeof(kAt) / sizeof(kAt[0]);
  if (byte <= kAt[0]) return kRead[0];
  if (byte >= kAt[kCount - 1]) return kRead[kCount - 1];
  int i = 1;
  while (kAt[i] < byte) ++i;
  const double t = static_cast<double>(byte - kAt[i - 1]) / (kAt[i] - kAt[i - 1]);
  // The settings were read an octave or so apart, so what sits between two of
  // them is their geometric mean and not their arithmetic one.
  return std::exp(std::log(kRead[i - 1]) + t * (std::log(kRead[i]) - std::log(kRead[i - 1])));
}

// 1 named setting(s) and one value for the rest
inline double pole0Sections(int byte) {
  if (byte == 1) return 1.0;
  return 0.0;
}

// 4 settings read, interpolated in log between them and flat outside them
inline double pole1CornerHz(int byte) {
  static const int kAt[] = {0, 8, 16, 24};
  static const double kRead[] = {242.596625483, 323.377429512, 401.638676356, 495.443771484};
  constexpr int kCount = sizeof(kAt) / sizeof(kAt[0]);
  if (byte <= kAt[0]) return kRead[0];
  if (byte >= kAt[kCount - 1]) return kRead[kCount - 1];
  int i = 1;
  while (kAt[i] < byte) ++i;
  const double t = static_cast<double>(byte - kAt[i - 1]) / (kAt[i] - kAt[i - 1]);
  // The settings were read an octave or so apart, so what sits between two of
  // them is their geometric mean and not their arithmetic one.
  return std::exp(std::log(kRead[i - 1]) + t * (std::log(kRead[i]) - std::log(kRead[i - 1])));
}

// 1 named setting(s) and one value for the rest
inline double pole1Sections(int byte) {
  if (byte == 2) return 1.0;
  return 0.0;
}

/** The chain the model names, in the order it names it. */
struct Effect {
  OnePole pole0[8];
  int poleCount0 = 0;
  OnePole pole1[8];
  int poleCount1 = 0;

  void prepare(int b40_03_04, int b40_03_03) {
    poleCount0 = static_cast<int>(pole0Sections(b40_03_03));
    if (poleCount0 > 8) poleCount0 = 8;
    const double poleCorner0 = pole0CornerHz(b40_03_04);
    for (int i = 0; i < poleCount0; ++i) {
      pole0[i].set(poleCorner0, OnePole::Side::Low, OnePole::Form::Bilinear);
    }
    poleCount1 = static_cast<int>(pole1Sections(b40_03_03));
    if (poleCount1 > 8) poleCount1 = 8;
    const double poleCorner1 = pole1CornerHz(b40_03_04);
    for (int i = 0; i < poleCount1; ++i) {
      pole1[i].set(poleCorner1, OnePole::Side::High, OnePole::Form::Bilinear);
    }
  }

  double process(double x) {
    for (int i = 0; i < poleCount0; ++i) x = pole0[i].process(x);
    for (int i = 0; i < poleCount1; ++i) x = pole1[i].process(x);
    return x;
  }
};
